audioscript.text: Part 1, you will hear a teaching assistant calling a country park about a school visit.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 1 to 6.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning, Hinchingbrooke Country Park, Sally speaking.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: I'm one of the rangers.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Oh, hello, uh, my name is John Chapman, and I'm a teaching assistant at a local primary school.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: I've been asked to arrange a visit to the park for two of our classes.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: OK, what would you like to know?
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Well, I'm new to this area.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: So perhaps you could tell me something about the park first, please.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Of course.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Altogether the park covers 170 acres.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: That's 69 hectares.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage directly states *'That's 69 hectares'* when describing the park's size. So the answer is **69**.

audioscript.text: There are three main types of habitat, wetland, grassland, and woodland.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: The woods are well established and varied.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: With an oak plantation and other areas of mixed species.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: The wetland is quite varied too.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: The original farmland was dug up around 40 years ago to extract gravel.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Once this work was completed, the gravel pits filled with water, forming the two large lakes.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: There are also several smaller ones.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Ponds and a stream that flows through the park.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage lists wetland features: *'Ponds and a stream that flows through the park'*. So the missing word is **stream**.

audioscript.text: OK, so I suppose with these different habitats, there's quite a variety of wildlife.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: There certainly is.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: A lot of different species of birds and insects, and also animals like deer and rabbits.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: And I understand you organize educational visits for school parties.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: We can organize a wide range of activities, and adapt them to suit all ages.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Can you give me some examples of the activities?
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Well, one focus is on science, where we help children to discover and study plants, trees and insects.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: They also collect and analyze data about the things they see.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q3: For science, the passage says children *'collect and analyze data about the things they see'*. So they look at **data**.

audioscript.text: Uh huh.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Another focus is on geography.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: The park is a great environment to learn and practice reading a map.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q4: The geography activity involves *'learning and practicing reading a map'*. So they learn to use a **map**.

audioscript.text: And using a compass to navigate around the park.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Do you do anything connected with history?
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Yes, we do.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: For instance, the children can explore how the use of the land has changed over time.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Then there's leisure and tourism.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: That focuses on your visitors, I would imagine.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Yes, mostly.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: The children find out about them, their requirements, the problems they may cause, and how we manage these.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q5: The leisure and tourism topic focuses on *'them'*, and the previous sentence asks about *'your visitors'*. So **'them'** means **visitors**.

audioscript.text: And another subject we cover is music.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Here the children experiment with natural materials to create sounds and explore rhythm and tempo.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q6: In music, children *'experiment with natural materials to create sounds'*. So they make **sounds**.

audioscript.text: That must be fun.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Most children really enjoy it.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: And of course, all the activities are educational too.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Learning outside the classroom encourages children to be creative and to explore and discover for themselves.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: I would imagine they get a sense of freedom that might not be a normal part of their lives.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage mentions children get *'a sense of freedom'* that is not normal for them. So the feeling is **freedom**.

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: And very often the children discover that they can do things they didn't know they could do.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: And they develop new skills.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says *'they develop new skills'*, which directly gives the answer **skills**.

audioscript.text: This gives them greater self-confidence.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: It sounds great.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: So what about the practical side of it?
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: How much does it cost for a full day visit?
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: We would expect to bring between 30 and 40 children
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: If there are over 30, it costs £4.95 for each child who attends on the day.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q9: The cost is stated as *'£4.95 for each child'* when there are over 30. So the answer is **4.95**.

audioscript.text: We invoice you afterwards, so you don't pay for children who can't come because of sickness, for example.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: There's no charge for leaders and other adults, as many as you want to bring.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says *'no charge for leaders and other adults'*, so adults like **leaders** are free.

audioscript.text: That sounds very fair.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: Well, thanks for all the information.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: I'll need to discuss it with my colleagues, and I hope to get back to you soon to make a booking.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: We'll look forward to hearing from you.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Goodbye.
audioscript.speaker: SALLY

audioscript.text: Goodbye, and thank you.
audioscript.speaker: JOHN

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Part 2, you will hear the chairman of Stanthorpe Twinning Association, which organizes the link between Stanthorpe in England and a town in France.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Talking to members about the year's events.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully, and answer questions 11 to 15.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: It's great to see so many members of the Twinning Association here tonight.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Since the twinning link between our two towns, Stanthorpe here in England, and Malatte in France was established, the relationship between the towns has gone from strength to strength.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Last month, 25 members of the association from Stanthorpe spent a weekend in Malatte.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Our hosts had arranged a great program.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We learned how cheese is produced in the region, and had the chance to taste the products.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The theme park trip had to be cancelled, but we all had a great time on the final boat trip down the river.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says *'the theme park trip had to be cancelled'*, so option A is wrong. Then it says *'we all had a great time on the final boat trip down the river'* and calls it *'the real highlight'* — **'highlight'** means the best part. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: That was the real highlight.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says *'the theme park trip had to be cancelled'*, so option A is wrong. Then it says *'we all had a great time on the final boat trip down the river'* and calls it *'the real highlight'* — **'highlight'** means the best part. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: This is a special year for the association, because it's 25 years since we were founded.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In Malatte, they're planning to mark this by building a footbridge in the municipal park.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We've been discussing what to do here, and we've decided to plant a Poplar tree in the museum gardens.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'we've decided to plant a Poplar tree in the museum gardens'* — a **'Poplar tree'** is a type of tree. They thought about a garden seat, but *'the authorities weren't happy with that idea'*, so option B is wrong. The footbridge is in France, not Stanthorpe. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: We considered buying a garden seat to put there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But the authorities weren't happy with that idea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In terms of fund raising to support our activities, we've done very well.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Our pancake evening was well attended and made record profits, and everyone enjoyed the demonstration of French cookery, which was nearly as successful.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says the pancake evening *'made record profits'* — **'record profits'** means it raised the most money. The cookery demonstration was *'nearly as successful'*, so it raised less. The film show had *'limited'* numbers, so it was not the top. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Numbers for our film show were limited because of the venue, so we're looking for somewhere bigger next year.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We're looking forward to welcoming our French visitors here next week.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And I know that many of you here will be hosting individuals or families.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The coach from France will arrive at 5 pm on Friday.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Don't try to do too much that first evening, as they'll be tired.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So have dinner in the house or garden rather than eating out.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says *'have dinner in the house or garden rather than eating out'* — **'rather than eating out'** means do NOT go to a restaurant. **'In the house or garden'** means at home. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: The weather looks as if it'll be OK, so you might like to plan a barbecue.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then the next morning's market day in town, and that's always a good place to stroll round.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On Saturday evening, we'll all meet up at the football club.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Where once again we'll have Toby Sharp and his band performing English and Scottish country songs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says on Saturday evening *'we'll have Toby Sharp and his band performing English and Scottish country songs'* — a band performing songs is a **concert**. There is no mention of a match or a competition. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Toby will already be well known to many of you, as last year he organized our special quiz night.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And presented the prizes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear an archaeology student giving a presentation on an important site in Ireland called the Céide Fields.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: For my presentation today, I'm going to talk about the Céide Fields in the northwest of Ireland, one of the largest Neolithic sites in the world.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I recently visited this site and observed the work that is currently being done by a team of archaeologists there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The site was first discovered in the 1930s by a local teacher, Patrick Caulfield.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He noticed that when local people were digging in the bog, they were constantly hitting against what seemed to be rows of stones.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He realized that these must be walls, and that they must be thousands of years old for them to predate the bog which subsequently grew over them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says Patrick Caulfield *'realized that these must be walls'* — the stones beneath the bog were once **walls**. So the answer is **walls**.

audioscript.text: He wrote to the National Museum in Dublin to ask them to investigate, but no one took him seriously.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It wasn't until 40 years later, when Patrick Caulfield's son Seamus, who had become an archaeologist by then, began to explore further.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'Patrick Caulfield's son Seamus, who had become an archaeologist'* — his **son** became the archaeologist. So the answer is **son**.

audioscript.text: He inserted iron probes into the bog, to map the formation of the stones.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A traditional method which local people had always used for finding fuel buried in the bog for thousands of years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says the traditional method was used *'for finding fuel buried in the bog'* — local people dug for **fuel**. So the answer is **fuel**.

audioscript.text: Carbon dating later proved that the site was over 5,000 years old, and was the largest Neolithic site in Ireland.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Thanks to the bog which covers the area, the remains of the settlement at Céide fields, which is over 5,000 years old, are extremely well preserved.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A bog is 90% water, its soil so saturated that when the grasses and heathers that grow on its surface die, they don't fully decay, but accumulate in layers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Objects remain so well preserved in these conditions because of the acidity of the peat, and the deficiency of oxygen.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says objects are well preserved because of *'the deficiency of oxygen'* — **'deficiency'** means a **lack**. So the answer is **oxygen**.

audioscript.text: At least 175 days of rain a year are required for this to happen.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This part of Ireland gets an average of 225 days.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Neolithic farmers at Céide would have enjoyed several centuries of relative peace and stability.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Neolithic farmers generally lived in larger communities than their predecessors.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: With a number of houses built around a community building.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As they lived in permanent settlements, Neolithic farmers were able to build bigger houses.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These weren't round as people often assume, but rectangular, with a small hole in the roof that allowed smoke to escape.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says the houses *'weren't round... but rectangular'* — the shape was **rectangular**, not round. So the answer is **rectangular**.

audioscript.text: This is one of many innovations, and indicates that the Neolithic farmers were the first people to cook indoors.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Another new technology that Neolithic settlers brought to Ireland was pottery.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Fragments of Neolithic pots have been found in Céide and elsewhere in Ireland.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The pots were used for many things, as well as for storing food.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Pots were filled with a small amount of fat, and when this was set alight, they served as lamps.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says pots with fat, when set alight, *'served as lamps'* — they were used to make **lamps**. So the answer is **lamps**.

audioscript.text: It's thought that the Céide fields were mainly used as paddocks for animals to graze in.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Evidence from the Céide fields suggests that each plot of land was of a suitable size, to sustain an extended family.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says each plot of land was a suitable size *'to sustain an extended family'* — it could support a big **family**. So the answer is **family**.

audioscript.text: Uh. They may have used a system of rotational grazing in order to prevent overgrazing and to allow for plant recovery and regrowth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This must have been a year-round activity, as no structures have been found which would have been used to shelter animals in the winter.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says no structures were found *'to shelter animals in the winter'* — there is no evidence of housing them during **winter**. So the answer is **winter**.

audioscript.text: However, archaeologists believe that this way of life at Céide ceased abruptly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Why was this?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, several factors may have contributed to the changing circumstances.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The soil would have become less productive, and led to the abandonment of farming.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says *'The soil would have become less productive'* — this means a decline in **soil** quality. So the answer is **soil**.

audioscript.text: The crop rotation system was partly responsible for this, as it would have been very intensive and was not sustainable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But there were also climatic pressures too.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The farmers at Céide would have enjoyed a relatively dry period, but this began to change, and the conditions became wetter as there was a lot more rain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says conditions became wetter *'as there was a lot more rain'* — this means an increase in **rain**. So the answer is **rain**.

audioscript.text: It was these conditions that encouraged the bog to form over the area, which survives today.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So now I'd like to show you some...
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a man called David talking on the radio about his work as a lifeboat volunteer.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.

audioscript.text: I never really planned to be a lifeboat volunteer when I came to live in Northsea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'd been working in London as a website designer, but although that was interesting,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I didn't like city life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'd been really keen on boats as a teenager, and I thought if I went to live by the sea, I might be able to pursue that interest a bit more in my free time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q11: Many students get confused because David had a job in London, but he didn't leave because of the job itself. The passage says he was *'really keen on boats as a teenager'* and wanted to *'pursue that interest'* — **'pursue an interest'** means to **develop a hobby**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Then, I found that the Lifeboat Institution was looking for volunteers, so I decided to apply.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Lifeboat Institution building here in Northsea's hard to miss.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's one of the largest in the country.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was built 15 years ago, with funds provided by a generous member of the public who'd lived here all her life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q12: The question asks who gave the money to build the station. The passage says funds were provided by a *'generous member of the public who'd lived here all her life'* — a **'member of the public'** who lived locally is a **local resident**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: As the Lifeboat Institution is a charity that relies on that kind of donation, rather than funding provided by the government, that was a huge help to us.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When I applied, I had to have a health assessment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The doctors were particularly interested in my vision.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I used to be short sighted, so I'd had to wear glasses, but I'd had laser eye surgery two years earlier, so that was OK.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They gave me tests for colour blindness, and they thought I might have a problem there, but it turned out I was OK.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q13: The doctor tested for a few things, but the passage says they *'thought I might have a problem there'* about **colour blindness**. ***Don't be trapped by 'short-sighted'*** — that was a past problem fixed by surgery. The concern was about **colour blindness**, so the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: When the coastguard gets an alert, all the volunteers are contacted and rush to the lifeboat station.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Our target's to get there in five minutes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then we try to get the boat off the dock and out to sea in another six to eight minutes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q14: The timing can be tricky because several numbers are mentioned. The passage says after arriving, they try to get the boat out to sea in *'another six to eight minutes'* — **'another'** means this is the time for launching, not the five-minute target to arrive. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: Our team's proud that we usually achieve that.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The average time across the country's eight and a half minutes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I've recently qualified as what's called a helmsman, which means I have the ultimate responsibility for the lifeboat.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I have to check that the equipment we use is in working order.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The crew have special life jackets that can support up to four people in the water, and it's ultimately my decision whether it's safe to launch the boat.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q15: As a helmsman, David has one key decision. The passage says it's *'ultimately my decision whether it's safe to launch the boat'* — this directly matches **if the lifeboat should be launched**. ***Don't be confused by equipment*** — he checks it, but the decision is about launching. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: But it's very rare not to launch it, even in the worst weather.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As well as going out on the lifeboat, my work involves other things too.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A lot of people underestimate how quickly conditions can change at sea, so I speak to youth groups and sailing clubs in the area.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: About the sorts of problems that sailors and swimmers can have, if the weather suddenly gets bad.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We also have a lot of volunteers who organize activities to raise money for us.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear a zoology student giving a presentation about an animal called tardigrade.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: For my project on invertebrates, I chose to study tardigrades.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These are microscopic, or to be more precise, near microscopic animals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There are well over 1,000 known species of these tiny animals, which belong to the phylum tardigrada.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Most tardigrades range in length from naught point naught five (0.05) to 1 millimetre.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Though the largest species can grow to be 1.2 millimeters in length, they are also sometimes called water bears, water because that's where they thrive best.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And bear because of the way they move.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says *'bear because of the way they move'* — so they are called water **'bears'** due to how they **move**. The answer is **move**.

audioscript.text: Moss piglet is another name for tardigrades, because of the way they look when viewed from the front.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They were first discovered in Germany in 1773 by Johann Goeze, who coined the name "Tardigrada".
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As I say, there are many different species of tardigrade, too many to describe here, but generally speaking, the different species share similar physical traits.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They have a body which is short and also rounded, a bit like a barrel.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage describes the body as *'short and also rounded, a bit like a barrel'* — so the body is **short** and round. The answer is **short**.

audioscript.text: And the body comprises four segments, each segment has a pair of legs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At the end of which are between four and 8 sharp claws.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I should also say that some species don't have any claws.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What they have are discs.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says some species don't have claws — *'What they have are discs'* — and these **discs** work by suction for gripping. The answer is **discs**.

audioscript.text: And these work by means of suction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They enable the tardigrade to cling on to surfaces or to grip its prey.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Within the body,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: there are no lungs or any organs for breathing at all.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Instead, oxygen and also blood are transported in a fluid that fills the cavity of the body.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'oxygen and also blood are transported in a fluid'* — so the liquid carries both **oxygen** and blood. The answer is **oxygen**.

audioscript.text: As far as the tardigrade's head is concerned, the best way I can describe this is that it looks rather strange - a bit squashed even - though many of the websites I looked at described its appearance as cute.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which isn't exactly very scientific.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The tardigrade's mouth is a kind of tube that can open outwards to reveal teeth-like structures known as "stylets".
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says *'The tardigrade's mouth is a kind of tube'* — so the mouth is shaped like a **tube**. The answer is **tube**.

audioscript.text: These are sharp enough to pierce plant or animal cells.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So where are tardigrades found?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Well, they live in every part of the world.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In a variety of habitats, most commonly on the bed of a lake, or on many kinds of plants, or in very wet environments.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There's been some interesting research which has found that tardigrades are capable of surviving radiation and very high pressure, and they're also able to withstand temperatures as cold as minus 200 degrees centigrade.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says they can *'withstand temperatures as cold as minus 200 degrees'* or *'highs of more than 148 degrees'* — so they exist in very low or high **temperatures**. The answer is **temperatures**.

audioscript.text: Or highs of more than 148 degrees centigrade, which is incredibly hot.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It has been said that tardigrades could survive long after human beings have been wiped out, even in the event of an asteroid hitting the earth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: If conditions become too extreme and tardigrades are at risk of drying out, they enter a state called cryptobiosis.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They curl into a ball called a tun.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That's t u n, by retracting their head and legs, and their metabolism drops to less than 1% of normal levels.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They can remain like this until they're reintroduced to water, when they will come back to life in a matter of a few hours, while in a state of cryptobiosis.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Tardigrades produce a protein that protects their DNA.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says *'Tardigrades produce a protein that protects their DNA'* — so a type of **protein** stops DNA damage. The answer is **protein**.

audioscript.text: In 2016, scientists revived two tardigrades that had been tuns for more than 30 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There was a report that, in 1948 a 120-year-old tun was revived, but this experiment has never been repeated.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There are currently several tests taking place in space to determine how long tardigrades might be able to survive there.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says *'several tests taking place in space'* to see how long they survive — so research is on survival in **space**. The answer is **space**.

audioscript.text: I believe the record so far is 10 days.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So moving on, in terms of their diet, tardigrades consume liquids in order to survive.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Although they have teeth, they don't use these for chewing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They suck the juices from moss or extract fluid from seaweed, but some species prey on other tardigrades, from other species or within their own.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says they *'extract fluid from seaweed'* — so they consume liquids found in moss or **seaweed**. The answer is **seaweed**.

audioscript.text: I suppose this isn't surprising given that tardigrades are mainly comprised of liquid and are coated with a type of gel.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Finally, I'd like to mention the conservation status of tardigrades.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It is estimated that they have been in existence for approximately half a billion years, and in that time, they have survived five mass extinctions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So it will probably come as no surprise to you that tardigrades have not been evaluated by the International Union for conservation of Nature, and are not on any endangered list.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says they are *'not on any endangered list'* — so they are not considered **endangered**. The answer is **endangered**.

audioscript.text: Some researchers have described them as thriving.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Does anyone have any questions they'd like to ask?
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.

audioscript.text: Hi, Jake.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: How are you getting on with the practical teaching?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.speaker: CLARE
audioscript.explain: Q21: Clare says her students *'don't seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives'* — this shows they have **no interest** in the subject. She also calls it *'depressing'*, which matches feeling **frustrated**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: It's depressing.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week, and the results weren't too bad, but there's no real engagement.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: I was wondering about something on the children's diets, you know, asking them to record what they eat, and maybe linking it to their state of health.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Hmm, let's think.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat, OK?
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But you'd also need to have access to the children's medical records.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q22: Jake says Clare would *'need to have access to the children's medical records'* and that *'confidentiality would be an issue'* — this means getting the data would be **difficult**. audioscript.text: And I don't think people would be happy about that, confidentiality would be an issue.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE
audioscript.explain: Q22: Jake says Clare would *'need to have access to the children's medical records'* and that *'confidentiality would be an issue'* — this means getting the data would be **difficult**. audioscript.text: If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it's not going to be easy.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Wouldn't that be upsetting for the children?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Well, the animals don't have to be harmed in any way.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: It could just be an experiment where they're given a certain diet and the effects are observed.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Yes, you'd have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: It's quite straightforward.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But if we found out that say a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn't necessarily be true for people, would it?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE
audioscript.explain: Q23: Clare asks if results from animals would be true for people, and Jake agrees *'that's true'* — they both accept that animal results **may not apply to humans**. The passage says getting permission is *'quite straightforward'*, so that is not a problem. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: No, that's true.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: But the findings for any experiment are going to be limited, it's inevitable.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: I suppose so.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: So what animals could I use to investigate the effect of diet?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Mice?
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Yes, you'd need experimental mice, ones that have been specially bred for experiments.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: Well, uh something to do with nutrition.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: So maybe we could look at food supplements, things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Hmm. That might be rather broad, maybe just look at the effects of one supplement like sugar on the health of the mice.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE

audioscript.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet.
audioscript.speaker: CLARE

audioscript.text: Exactly.

audioscript.text: Great.

audioscript.text: And how would I tell them apart?

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental science lecture about microplastics.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to be talking about microplastics.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic smaller than 5 millimeters in size.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Recently, there's been a greater awareness that there are large quantities of plastic waste big and small.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the environment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The amount of plastic waste in the oceans has received widespread attention, but far less is known about the effects of microplastics in fresh water.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And particularly in soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Microplastics can enter the environment via a number of different sources.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Threads and microfibers detached from synthetic clothing every time they're put in a washing machine, and these find their way into the water system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The question asks about fibres from some **'clothing'** during washing. The passage says *'threads and microfibers detached from synthetic clothing every time they're put in a washing machine'*. So the answer is **clothing**.

audioscript.text: Other sources include big pieces of plastic waste that are already in the environment, and these break down into microscopic particles over a period of time.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: On a larger scale, factory waste is another route, as are tyres, which wear down as cars, lorries, and so on, travel along road surfaces.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: We already understand some of the impacts of microplastics from studies involving fish and other animals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There is evidence that microplastics harm small creatures in a variety of ways.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as by damaging their mouths or by impairing their ability to feed, for example, when microplastics get lodged in their digestive system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The question says microplastics cause injuries to the **'mouths'** of wildlife. The passage directly states they harm creatures *'by damaging their mouths'*. So the answer is **mouths**.

audioscript.text: Surprisingly, perhaps, it is likely that humans consume microplastics.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As these have been detected in a wide range of food and drink products, including bottled water.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As well as in water that comes direct from the tap.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What's more, salt and many kinds of seafood have also been found to contain microplastics.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The question lists examples of food containing microplastics, including **'salt'**. The passage says *'salt and many kinds of seafood have also been found to contain microplastics'*. So the answer is **salt**.

audioscript.text: However, it's important to underline that there is not yet conclusive proof that microplastics cause significant harm to people.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In many countries, including here in the UK, there is legislation which prevents manufacturers from adding plastic microbeads to shower gels, facial cleansers and toothpaste.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The question says microplastics are banned in skin cleaning products and **'toothpaste'**. The passage mentions legislation preventing microbeads in *'shower gels, facial cleansers and toothpaste'*. So the answer is **toothpaste**.

audioscript.text: It is very difficult to accurately estimate the total amount of microplastic particles in the soil, as they can be hard to detect.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But we do know they are carried in the air.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And deposited in the soil by rain.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: What's more, many of the fertilizers used by both farmers and gardeners contain microplastics.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The question asks how microplastics enter soil, including through **'fertilisers'** (or **'fertilizers'**). The passage says *'many of the fertilizers used by both farmers and gardeners contain microplastics'*. So the answer is **fertilisers** or **fertilizers**.

audioscript.text: A team from the Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge has carried out a study of the effects of microplastics on the digestive tracts of earthworms.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These worms, which live in topsoil, are an essential component of our agricultural system.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: By feeding on soil, they mix nutrients into it, thereby making it more fertile.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The question says earthworms are important because they add **'nutrients'** to the soil. The passage explains they *'mix nutrients into it, thereby making it more fertile'*. So the answer is **nutrients**.

audioscript.text: The researchers set out to discover whether the introduction of microplastics into the soil and the subsequent ingestion of these by earthworms would impact soil quality.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And ultimately inhibit plant growth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The question asks if microplastics affect the **'growth'** of plants. The passage says the study aimed to see if microplastics would *'ultimately inhibit plant growth'*. So the answer is **growth**.

audioscript.text: The short answer was yes, it did.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After placing three different types of microplastic particles into the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They planted perennial ryegrass.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The particles of microplastic, which included biodegradable PLA, and conventional high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, were then ingested by the earthworms in the soil.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The result was that the worms lost weight rapidly.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The question says microplastics caused **'weight'** loss in earthworms. The passage states *'the result was that the worms lost weight rapidly'*. So the answer is **weight**.

audioscript.text: What's more, a lower percentage than normal of the ryegrass seeds germinated.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And the researchers concluded that this was a direct result of the earthworms being unable to fulfill their normal role in making soil more fertile.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The team also discovered that there was an increase in the amount of acid found in the soil, and this was attributed mainly to the microplastic particles from conventional HDPE plastic.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The question says there was a rise in the level of **'acid'** in the soil. The passage reports *'an increase in the amount of acid found in the soil'*. So the answer is **acid**.

audioscript.text: The conclusions of the study make for very interesting reading.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I've included the reference in the notes to give you at the end of this session.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To summarize, the authors proposed the idea that we need to regard soil as we would regard any other process in nature.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This means we should accept the implications of soil being dependent on decaying and dead matter.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Constantly being passed through the bodies of earthworms.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is when soil becomes impoverished by the presence of microplastics, not only ecosystems but also the whole of society are negatively impacted.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The question says changes to soil damage both ecosystems and **'society'**. The passage concludes that *'not only ecosystems but also the whole of society are negatively impacted'*. So the answer is **society**.

audioscript.text: That is the end of part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Welcome to my podcast.

audioscript.text: If you're thinking about taking up running, I'm here to help.
audioscript.speaker: LIZ FULLER

audioscript.text: There are many training programs available online, which aim to help people build up to running 5 kilometers.
audioscript.speaker: LIZ FULLER

audioscript.text: Some of them are great, and thousands of people of all ages are taking part in 5 kilometer races across the country as a result.
audioscript.speaker: LIZ FULLER

audioscript.text: People like them because they're easy to follow, and don't push them too hard.
audioscript.speaker: LIZ FULLER

audioscript.text: Yeah, that's obvious.

audioscript.text: He also told me to pack them flat in the box, not on their side.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Again because they can bend, and if you leave them like that for, say, a year.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: It's quite hard to get them back to their normal shape.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: Well, it's pretty clear that ruins them, but a lot of people just can't be bothered to protect their books.

audioscript.text: He always says it's such a shame that publishers don't use better quality paper.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: It's the acid in the paper that causes the problem, isn't it?
audioscript.speaker: KIERAN

audioscript.text: Yeah, that's why old books go yellow.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: You know, some of the books my grandfather's given me are like that already.
audioscript.speaker: JANE

audioscript.text: I should dump them really, if they're going to deteriorate further, but I'd feel bad.

audioscript.text: They'll always remind me of him, he's quite a collector you know.

audioscript.text: Yeah, they're different, I suppose.

audioscript.text: But I still don't think people value hardbacks like they used to.

audioscript.text: Part 4, you will hear part of an environmental studies lecture on tree planting.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Tree planting now dominates political and popular agendas, and is often presented as an easy answer to the climate crisis, as well as a way for business corporations to offset their carbon emissions.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But unfortunately, tree planting isn't as straightforward as some people think.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: When the wrong trees are planted in the wrong place, it can do considerably more damage than good.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Failing to help either people or the environment.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Reforestation projects are currently being undertaken on a huge scale in many countries, and it's crucial that the right trees are selected.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A mix of species should always be planted, typical of the local natural forest ecosystem, and including rare and endangered species in order to create a rich ecosystem.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's important to avoid non-native species that could become invasive.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Invasive species are a significant contributor to the current global biodiversity crisis.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And are often in competition with native species, and may threaten their long-term survival.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says invasive species are *'often in competition with native species'* — the question asks for the possible result of not avoiding them. So the answer is **competition**.

audioscript.text: Restoring biodiversity that will maximize carbon capture is key when reforesting an area, but ideally any reforestation project should have several goals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These could include selecting trees that can contribute to wildlife conservation, improve the availability of food for the local community, and maintain the stability of soil systems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage lists goals like *'improve the availability of food for the local community'* — **'availability of food'** means a **sustainable source of food**. So the answer is **food**.

audioscript.text: Meeting as many of these goals as possible, whilst doing no harm to local communities, native ecosystems and vulnerable species, is the sign of a highly successful tree-planting scheme.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To ensure the survival and resilience of a planted forest, it's vital to use tree seeds with appropriate levels of genetic diversity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The amount of genetic variation found within a species is essential for their survival.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Using seeds with low genetic diversity generally lowers the resilience of restored forests, which can make them vulnerable to disease, and unable to adapt to climate change.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says low diversity makes forests *'vulnerable to disease'* — **'vulnerable'** means low resistance. So high diversity increases resistance to **disease**.

audioscript.text: Choosing the right location for reforestation projects is as important as choosing the right trees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ultimately, the best area for planting trees would be formerly forested areas that are in poor condition.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's better to avoid non-forested landscapes, such as natural grasslands, savannas or wetlands.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As these ecosystems already contribute greatly to capturing carbon, it would also be advantageous to choose an area where trees could provide other benefits.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as recreational spaces, reforesting areas which are currently exploited for agriculture should be avoided.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says to avoid *'areas which are currently exploited for agriculture'* — **'exploited for'** means **used for**. So the answer is **agriculture**.

audioscript.text: As this often leads to other areas being deforested.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Large scale reforestation projects require careful planning.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Making the right decisions about where to plant trees depends on having the right information.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Having detailed and up-to-date maps, identifying high-priority areas for intervention is essential.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says *'detailed and up-to-date maps'* are essential for planning — **'detailed and up-to-date'** means **accurate**. So the answer is **maps**.

audioscript.text: Drone technology is a useful tool in helping to prioritize and monitor areas of degraded forest for restoration, in Brazil, it's being used to identify and quantify how parts of the Amazon are being devastated by human activities.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Such as rearing cattle and illegal logging.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage lists *'rearing cattle and illegal logging'* as harmful activities — **'rearing'** means **keeping** animals. So the answer is **cattle**.

audioscript.text: A good example of where the right trees were picked to achieve a restored forest is in Lampang province in northern Thailand.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: A previously forested site which had been degraded through mining was reforested by a cement company together with Chiang Mai University.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After spreading 60 cm of top soil, they planted 14 different native tree species, which included several species of fig.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Figs are a keystone species, because of the critical role they play in maintaining wildlife populations.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: They are central to tropical reforestation projects.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As they accelerate the speed of the recovery process by attracting animals and birds, which act as natural seed dispersers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says figs *'accelerate the speed of the recovery process'* — **'accelerate'** means **increase**. So the answer is **speed**.

audioscript.text: This helps to promote diversity through the healthy regrowth of a wide range of plant species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Unlike the majority of fruit trees, figs bear fruit all year round, providing a reliable food source for many species.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: At this site for example, after only three rainy seasons, monkeys started visiting to eat the fig fruits, naturally dispersing seeds through defecation.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage gives an example: *'monkeys started visiting to eat the fig fruits'* — they were attracted to the area. So the answer is **monkeys**.

audioscript.text: Reforestation projects should always aim to make sure that local communities are consulted and involved in the decision making process.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The restoration of mangrove forests in Madagascar is an example of a project which has succeeded in creating real benefits for the community.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Destruction of the mangrove forests had a terrible impact on plant and animal life, and also badly affected the fishing industry.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which was a major source of employment for local people living in coastal areas, the reforestation project involved hiring local people.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: To plant and care for the new mangrove trees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Millions of mangrove trees have now been planted, which has resulted in the return of a healthy aquatic ecosystem.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The mangroves also act as a defense against the increased threat of flooding caused by climate change.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says mangroves defend against *'the increased threat of flooding'* — **'increased threat'** means **higher risk**. So the answer is **flooding**.

audioscript.text: What's more, the local economy is more stable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And thousands more Madagascans are now able to send their children to school.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One other important point to consider.
